mechaber.he:
המחליף פרה בחמור או שקנה ונמצא נקב בבית הכוסות. ובו ב סעיפים:
כל מי שנולד ספק ברשותו עליו להביא ראיה כיצד המחליף פרה בחמור ומשך בעל החמור את הפרה ולא הספיק בעל הפרה למשוך החמור עד שמת החמור על בעל החמור להביא ראיה שהי' חמורו קיים בשעת משיכת הפרה וכן כל כיוצא בזה: הגה וי"א דעל בעל הפרה להביא ראיה דמאחר שקנה החמור בכל מקום שהוא הרי היה ברשות בעל הפרה ועליו להביא ראיה כמו שיתבאר בסמוך לענין טבח (טור בשם הרא"ש) ואם אינו מביא ראיה ישבע המוכר שלא ידע המומין אלו ופטור (מרדכי פרק המדיר) ראובן החליף עם שמעון סוס ביין וכאשר משך שמעון הסוס בא עכו"ם ולקחו ממנו ואמר שהסוס נגנב ממנו ורוצה שמעון להחזיק ביין שבידו אם ראובן מודה שנגנב הסוס הוי מקח טעות ויוכל שמעון להחזיק מה שבידו אבל אם ראובן אינו מודה אמרינן העכו"ם משקר וצריך לתת היין לראובן (מרדכי פרק הזהב ותשובת מיימוני דקנין סימן ו'):
mechaber.en:
One who exchanges a cow for a donkey, or purchases an animal later found perforated in the reticulum. It contains two seifim.
Whenever a doubt arises while property is in a person's possession, that person bears the burden of proof. Thus, if one exchanges a cow for a donkey, the owner of the donkey performs meshichah on the cow, and before the owner of the cow performs meshichah on the donkey the donkey dies, the owner of the donkey must prove that it was alive when he took possession of the cow. The same rule applies in similar cases. Rama: Some say the owner of the cow bears the burden of proof, because upon his acquisition the donkey became his wherever it stood, and the doubt arose in his possession. If he cannot prove his claim, the seller swears that he did not know of the defect and is exempt. Reuven exchanged a horse with Shimon for wine. After Shimon took the horse, a non-Jew seized it, claiming it had been stolen from him. Shimon wishes to retain the wine. If Reuven admits the horse was stolen, the transaction was erroneous and Shimon may retain what he holds. If Reuven denies it, we assume the non-Jew's claim is false, and Shimon must deliver the wine to Reuven.

baer_hetev.he:
החמור. אינו ר"ל שמת קודם משיכת בעל הפרה להחמור דא"כ ליכא מאן דפליג דההפסד הוא לבעל הפרה דהא מיד כשמשך בעל החמור את הפרה נקנה החמור לבעל הפרה ובמזלו מת אלא ה"ק ולא הספיק למשוך את החמור עד שמצאו מת ואינו ידוע אימתי מת אם קודם משיכת הפרה או אח"כ וכ"כ הטור. סמ"ע:
הפרה. דס"ל כיון שנולד הספק (היינו שנתוודע מיתתו) אחר המשיכה בזמן שהיה בחזקת בעל הפרה עליו הראיה ואי לא מוקמינן אחזקת שהיה חי כמו שהי' בראשונ' והא דלא אמרינן כן בר"ס שלפני זה במחליף פרה בחמור כו' וילדה ואינו ידוע אם קודם המשיכה ילדה הפרה או אח"כ דהל"ל כיון דבשעת משיכת הפרה היתה בחזקת בעל החמור ובחזקת שהית' מעוברת ואח"כ נולד הספק שאינה מעוברת נוקמא בחזקת מעוברת כמו שהיתה מקודם לכן דדוקא כאן דהחליף החמור בפרה ידוע ובמשיכת הפרה זכה הלה בחמור מש"ה מקרי עומד ברשותו משא"כ התם בילדה הפרה ומחולקים בהולד דלעולם לא נתברר אי הוה הולד בכלל הקנין די"ל שלא תלד ולד קיימא או שלא נתעברה ונתקיים הקנין זולת הולד עכ"ל הסמ"ע (והט"ז כת' דקושיא מעיקרא ליתא דאשתמיטתיה דברי התוספות בפ' המדיר וז"ל וצריך לחלק בין ספק שנולד לטיבותא כי התם לספק שנולד לריעותא כי הכא ע"כ) א"ה במחילת כבוד הרב ט"ז ז"ל חשד בכשרים שנעלם מהסמ"ע דברי התוספות אלו והרי הביאה בפרישה רק שכתב דנראה לחלק גם בכה"ג ע"ש ותמצא:
baer_hetev.en:
The worst. It is not a Rashi who first died of a cow’s attraction to the expropriation of the husband of the victim to the husband of the cow, but rather the “c” and did not attract the grave until he found a dead man and was not known if he had previously withdrawn the breach or so as the column. A:
The cow. The reasoning is that since the doubt arose (meaning, the death became known) only after meshichah, at a time when the cow was in the possession of the owner of the cow, that owner bears the burden of proof. If he cannot prove his claim, we preserve the prior presumption that the animal was alive as before. Why do we not say the same at the beginning of the preceding siman, where one exchanged a cow for a donkey and the cow gave birth, and it is unknown whether she gave birth before or after meshichah? There, one might say that at the time of meshichah the cow was in the possession of the donkey's owner and had the presumption of being pregnant; when doubt later arose because she was no longer pregnant, we should preserve her prior presumption of pregnancy. The distinction is that here he exchanged the donkey for a particular known cow, and through meshichah of the cow the other party acquired the donkey. Therefore the animal is considered to have been in his possession. In the earlier case, however, where the cow gave birth and they dispute the offspring, it was never established whether the offspring was included in the acquisition at all, for perhaps she would not produce a viable offspring, or perhaps she was not pregnant, so the acquisition could have taken effect without the offspring. Sema. Taz writes that the question does not arise at all, because Sema overlooked Tosafot in HaMadir, who distinguish between a doubt that arises in a favorable direction there and a doubt that arises to the detriment here. With due respect to Taz, he suspected the innocent. Sema did not overlook these Tosafot, for he cites them in Perishah. He merely writes that one can distinguish the cases even in the manner he proposed. See there.

beer_hagolah.he: א) ל' הרמב"ם בפ"כ מהלכות מכירה דין י"ד וכתב ה"ה מימרא דרב יהודה אמר שמואל בכתובות פרק המדיר (כתובות דף ע"ו ע"א) ולזה נוטה דעת הרי"ף וכ' הכ"מ דאין לנו בזה אלא מ"ש הר"ן בשם הר"ז שפי' דרב יהודה ס"ל דאותו שנולד הספק בממונו עליו הראיה וחמור ממונו של בעל החמור מקרי וכו' ואלו לרמי בר יחזקאל שם ע"ב כיון שלא נולד הספק ברשותו אלא ברשות בעל הפרה על בעל הפרה להביא ראיה משום דאמרינן כאן נמצא וכאן מת וכו' וכאן שמת בבית בעל החמור כולהו מודו דעליו הראיה כו' וכ"כ ה"ה בשם קצת מפורשים דלא אמרי' הכי אלא כשמת החמור ברשות בעל החמור ובעל החמור אינו טוען ברי שהיה חי בשעת משיכת הפרה הא אם היה טוען ברי או שהיה החמור באגם על בעל הפרס להביא ראיה וכתבו הרשב"א והרמב"ן שצ"ע על הרי"ף ז"ל שלא חלק בזה כלל:
beer_hagolah.en: Alef) This is the language of the Rambam, chapter 20 of Hilkhot Mekhirah, halachah 14. The Maggid Mishneh cites the statement of Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel in Ketubot 76a and writes that the Rif inclines to this view. The Kesef Mishneh writes that we have only the Ran's explanation in the name of the Baal HaMaor: Rav Yehudah holds that the person in whose property the uncertainty arose bears the burden of proof, and the donkey is considered the property of the donkey's owner. According to Rami bar Yechezkel on 76b, however, because the doubt did not arise in his domain but in the cow owner's domain, the cow owner must bring proof, based on the principle that the defect is presumed to have arisen where it is presently found. Where the donkey died in the donkey owner's house, all agree that he bears the burden of proof. The Maggid Mishneh cites some commentators who say that this applies specifically where the donkey died in its owner's domain and the owner does not make a definite claim that it was alive at the time the cow was drawn. But if he makes such a definite claim, or if the donkey was in a marsh, the cow owner bears the burden of proof. The Rashba and Ramban write that the Rif's failure to distinguish these cases requires study.

beur_hagra.he:
כל מי כו'. כפי' הרי"ף שם וראיה לפי' מדפריך בב"מ ק' א' וניחזי ברשותא דמאן כו':
וי"א כו'. כפירש"י שם ועתוס' שם ד"ה כל הנולד כו' וראיה לפי' זה מדאמר לא תציתו ליה כו' מ' דפליג עליו:
ואם אינו כו'. כמו מנה לי בידך והלה אומר איני יודע ואע"ג דכאן גם שכנגדו אינו יודע משבעינן על טענת ספק כמו המכיר כליו וספריו והמוציא על נכסי אשתו וחנוני על פנקסו דכל שיש רגלים לדבר צריך לישבע אף על טענת ספק וע"ל סי' ע"ה סי"ז בהג"ה וכמ"ש משביעין אותו שאינו ברשותו וכן כאן דה"ל לידע אם היה בו מום או לא:
אם ראובן מודה כו'. כמ"ש בב"ב מ"ד ב' דאף רב זביד ל"ק אלא בשלא באחריות:
אבל אם כו'. כמ"ש שם מ"ה א' אמימר אמר כו' וא"צ אפי' שבועה דאין נשבעין על טענת שמא בשאין רגלים לדכר כמ"ש בפ' כל הנשבעין ואלו נשבעין כו' וכמש"ל סי' ע"ה סי"ז בש"ע וכ"ש כאן דסתם עכו"ם אנסין הן וע"ל סי' קע"ו סל"ו בהג"ה:
beur_hagra.en:
Every person, etc. This follows Rif's explanation. Proof comes from Bava Metzia 100a, where the Gemara asks in whose possession the object stands.
Some say, etc. This follows Rashi. See Tosafot there, s.v. Every item born, and the proof from the statement, 'Do not heed him,' which indicates disagreement.
If not so. As Hashem tells me, I don't know, and I'm not sure if he does not know what he is saying about his words and his books, and he's given his wife's possessions, and he's given his book, and he's got to swear to him, and he's not allowed to know him
If Reuven concedes, etc. As stated in Bava Batra 44b, even Rav Zevid disagrees only where the property was sold without responsibility.
But if he's called. A. A. A. A. A. A. A. A. A. A. A. A. A. A. A. A. I.A. said, “I swear to you that you are not allowed to do so, and that you swear to them, and that you will be saved.”

chokhmat_shlomo.he: סעיף א' וי"א כו'. נ"ב הנה אם לקח חפץ מחברו ונמצא בו כתם וכדומה ולא נודע אצל מי נעשה הכתם אצל הראשון או אצל השני ונ"מ הוצאות הכביסה על מי חל. דבר זה יש ללמוד מן הש"ס ותוס' בנדה דנ"ח וד"ה ולענין דינא תנן. שהקשו שם דנימא כל שנולד הספק ברשותה עליו הראיה. דתירצו כיון דאינו ממש שלה רק שאול בידה לא נחשב ברשותה ממש. ועוד תירצו דהתם אם ירצו להוציא צריך להביא ראיה אבל הכא לא תתחייב האחרונה לכבס. והנה תירוץ השני תמי' לי מאד דהמעיין בכל הסוגית דהי' בה מומין שם גבי המחליף פרה מוכח דאמרי' כל שנולד' הספק ברשותו אפי' אם בא להחזיק צריך להביא ראיה וכן קיי"ל הכא ועיין שם בסוגיא להדיא והאיך כתבו דוקא להוציא ולכך העיקר כתירוץ הראשון ולכך מוכח שאם קנתה כה"ג על השני' לכבסו אף אם עדיין לא נתנה דמי המקח או שהוא מוחזק מצד אחד בממון המוכר מ"מ כיון שנולד ברשותו עליו לכבסו. אבל אם בשאלה אירע כה"ג מוכח מדבריכם הנ"ל דבשאלה לא אמרי' כל שנולד הספק ברשותו רק בזה פטור מספק וא"כ אם שאל חפץ או בכמה מחברו ואח"כ נמצא בו מום שלא נודע אימת נעשה פטור השואל כדמוכח מש"ס ותוס' הנ"ל. ותירוצם השני צ"ע ועיין בפסקי תוס' שם העתיק לדינא רק התירוץ הראשון לבד וז"ב: שוב הגיע לידי אחר כמה שנים ספר סדרי טהרה על נדה והרגיש בתמי' זו ועיין בחיבורי מי נדה לפרש דבריהם על נכון עיי"ש מה שיוציא משם לדינא לכאן:
chokhmat_shlomo.en: Seif 1. And some say, etc. Note: If one buys an article from another and a stain or similar defect is later found, but it is unknown whether it arose while the article was with the first owner or the second, determining who bears the cleaning expense can be learned from Niddah 58 and Tosafot there, s.v. "and regarding the law we learned." Tosafot ask why we do not apply the rule that whenever a doubt arises while the property is in someone's domain, that person bears the burden of proof. They answer first that because the garment is merely borrowed and is not actually hers, it is not considered fully within her domain. They also answer that the rule applies only where someone seeks to extract money, whereas in that case the later borrower is merely being asked to wash the garment. Their second answer is very difficult. Throughout the sugya of defects and the case of one who exchanges a cow, the rule that a doubt arising in a person's domain places the burden upon him applies even where he seeks only to retain money rather than extract it, and this is the practical ruling here. The principal answer is therefore Tosafot's first answer. It follows that where the article was actually purchased, the later purchaser must pay for cleaning even if he has not yet paid the purchase price or happens to possess other money belonging to the seller. Because the doubt arose in his domain, the burden rests upon him. But if the article was only borrowed, the cited Tosafot proves that the rule does not apply, and the borrower is exempt because of the doubt. Thus if one borrows an article or animal and a defect is later found, with no knowledge of when it arose, the borrower is exempt. Tosafot's second answer requires study. Years later I obtained the work Sidrei Taharah on Niddah and found that he too noticed this difficulty. See my work Mei Niddah, where I explained Tosafot properly and derived the practical rule relevant here.

ketzot_hachoshen.he: ישבע המוכר שלא ידע המומין וכ' במרדכי פ' המדיר דליכא להימניה ללוקח במגו כי לא יהיב דמי שיאמר ברשות המוכר נולדה המום במגו דאי בעי אמר פרעתיך שהרי אינה טענה ודאי דא"כ הרי ידע המום קודם לכן וסבר וקבל הלכך לעולם לא מהימן במגו עכ"ל ובשלטי גבורים פ' האומנין כ' עלה ז"ל וקשי' לי על דברי המרדכי במה שאמר ואם טען טענה ודאי ברשותך נולד הרי סבר וקיבל וכי אי אפשר להיות שזה יתגלה לו עתה ע"י עדים שמצא עתה שמום זה הי' בבהמה זו קודם שמכרה לו המוכר והוא לא ידע בהאי שעתא שלקחו וא"כ הדרא קושיא לדוכתיה ליפטר לוקח בטענתו במגו דאי בעי אמר פרעתיך וצ"ע עכ"ל. ואינו קושיא דודאי אפי' שמע מפי מאה עדים שאמרו לו שהיה בו המום קודם כל זמן שלא נחקרה עדותן בב"ד ובפני בע"ד וכל שעדיין לא העידו בב"ד לא הוי טענת ברי על פיהם אלא לענין שבועה דיכול להשביע ע"פ שמועה ששמע אפי' מפי קרוב אלא אם טוען העמדתיך בדין והעידו עדים בב"ד בפניו או שלא בפניו במקום שמקבלין עדים שלא בפני בע"ד כגון שהיו עדיו חולים וכל כה"ג ודאי מהימן במגו אלא דהמרדכי לא איירי מזה אך קשה בהא דכ' הרמב"ם וטור וש"ע סי' קכ"ו סעיף י"ב ז"ל טען שהי' עני והטעהו כו' ואם הוא מלוה בשטר נשבע שהי' עני והטעהו ונוטל ע"ש ולפמ"ש במרדכי לא משכחת טענת ברי בטענת מקח ומטעמ' שכ' דא"כ סבר וקיבל ואולי שם יותר משכחת לה בטענת ברי וכגון שנודע לו אח"כ שהספינה או הסחורה והחובות נאבדו ונתקלקלו:
ketzot_hachoshen.en: The seller shall swear that he did not know of the defects. Mordechai says the purchaser cannot be believed through a migo that, had he wished, he could have said, "I have not paid," and then assert definitively that the defect arose in the seller's domain. If the purchaser truly knew that the defect existed before the sale, then he must also have known of it at the time of purchase and is treated as having accepted it. His claim cannot ordinarily be a definite one. Shiltei Gibborim objects that perhaps the purchaser only now learned through witnesses that the defect had already existed before the sale. He personally did not know it at purchase. If so, why should he not make a definite claim now and rely on the migo of nonpayment? This is not a difficulty. Even if he heard the fact from one hundred witnesses, so long as their testimony has not been formally received in beit din before the opposing party, their statements do not become his own definite factual knowledge for litigation. They can suffice as a basis for requiring an oath, even if the information came from a relative, but not to create a definite plea in his own mouth. If he says, however, that the matter was already litigated and witnesses testified in beit din, either before the seller or in one of the recognized situations where testimony can be received in his absence, then he can indeed make the definite claim and can use the migo. Mordechai was not addressing such a case. A difficulty remains from Rambam, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch in siman 126, where one who says that the debtor was already poor and the other deceived him can, with a written loan, swear that fact and collect. According to Mordechai's reasoning, how can such a definite plea arise? Perhaps that case more readily allows later definite knowledge, such as learning conclusively that the ship, merchandise, or debts had already been lost or ruined before the transfer.

meirat_einayim.he:
עד שמת החמור. אינו ר"ל שמת אחר משיכת בעל החמור את הפרה וקודם משיכת בעל הפרה להחמור דא"כ ליכא מאן דפליג דההפסד הוא לבעל הפרה דהא מיד כשמשך בעל החמור הפרה נקנ' החמור לבעל הפרה ובמזלו מת אלא ה"ק ולא הספיק למשוך החמור עד שמצאו מת ואינו ידוע אימתי מת אם קודם משיכת הפרה או אח"כ וכ"כ בטור:
על בעל החמור כו'. הטעם דס"ל כאן נמצא כאן היה ואמרינן שבעודו בחזקתו דהיינו קודם שמשך הפרה מת אם לא שיביא ראייה שאחר המשיכה מת ומה"ט נמי מסיק הטור בשם הרי"ף שהוא ג"כ בעל סברא זו דהיינו דוקא אם עומד החמור בבית בעל החמור בשעת מיתה אבל אם מת באגם הראיה הוא על הפרה דבכה"ג ליכא למימר כאן נמצא כאן היה:

The view here is that since the doubt arose, meaning the death became known, only after the meshichah, at a time when the object was under the presumption of the owner of the cow, the burden of proof rests upon him. If he cannot prove it, we maintain the animal's prior presumption of life. In the Perishah I explained why we do not say the same at the beginning of the preceding siman, where one exchanges a cow for a donkey, the owner of the cow pulls the donkey, the cow gives birth, and it is unknown whether the birth occurred before or after the meshichah. One might argue there too that at the time the donkey was pulled the cow belonged to the donkey owner and was presumed pregnant, so when the doubt later arose we should maintain the prior presumption that it remained pregnant until after the transaction. I distinguished the cases. Here the donkey was exchanged for a specific known cow, and when the cow was pulled the other party definitively acquired the donkey. The donkey is therefore considered to have stood in his ownership. In the prior case, however, the dispute concerns the offspring itself, and it was never established that the offspring was included in the transaction. The cow might not have produced a viable offspring, or might not have been pregnant at all, while the transaction could still have taken effect without the offspring. See the Perishah for another distinction.

The owner of the donkey must bring proof. The reason is that here it was found and here it is presumed to have arisen. This applies specifically where it stands in the possession of the donkey's owner, but if it stands in a meadow, the owner of the cow must bring proof (Sema).
And there are those who say that the owner of the cow must bring proof. They maintain that since the uncertainty arose after meshichah, when the item was already in the domain of the cow's owner, and the presumption of continued life also supports the donkey's owner, the cow's owner must therefore bring proof. This reasoning applies specifically here, where the uncertainty arose to the detriment of the cow's owner while the item was in his domain. But if the uncertainty arose to his advantage, such as above in siman 223 concerning one who exchanges a cow for a donkey and the cow gives birth, we do not apply the rule that every uncertainty arising in one's domain is charged against him, Tosafos, Ketubot 75. See Beurim: the rule is not limited to death; the same applies if the item was stolen or lost. See there also regarding two partners who divided property and afterward a deficiency was found in the share of one of them.

pitchei_teshuva.en: The burden is upon the owner of the donkey. See Sema, through his statement that if the donkey died in a meadow the burden of proof is upon the owner of the cow. Responsa Avodat HaGershuni, siman 87, discusses Reuven's sale to Shimon of one hundred kor of grain at one dinar per kor. Shimon paid twenty dinars, was to pay the balance within eight days, and could take delivery within fourteen days. He later paid further sums but retained an amount against the possibility that the full hundred kor would not be present, and Reuven agreed. Reuven then told him to remove the grain because the owner of the loft would no longer store it. Shimon told him to send whomever he wished to move it to another loft. Reuven sent an agent, and when Shimon later came to take the grain twenty kor were missing. Reuven claimed that any loss occurred after delivery to Shimon through Shimon's agent and demanded the balance; Shimon denied this. At first glance, if Shimon admitted Reuven's account, the rule that the party in whose domain the doubt arose bears the burden of proof would place the burden on Shimon, since the doubt arose after the agent moved the grain. Yet the responsum concludes otherwise. We do not know that one hundred kor were present when the agent took possession, because the grain had never been measured. The seller's assertion cannot itself establish a prior presumption. This differs from an animal whose prior sound condition is known and where the rule "here it was found, here it arose" can operate. Accordingly, the purchaser need not pay the amount he retained. If, however, the seller holds money exceeding the price of the eighty kor unquestionably delivered, the purchaser cannot extract it merely on a doubtful claim while the seller asserts with certainty that the full amount was present; the seller need not swear to the quantity corresponding to money already in his possession, though a general ban may be imposed. Shav Yaakov, Choshen Mishpat, end of siman 6, challenges Avodat HaGershuni in light of the Shach in siman 91. Where an agent was appointed to make delivery, there is a presumption that the agent performed his mission. Even if the agent denies finding the full quantity while the seller states certainly that it was there, the seller should at least collect with an oath, like a shopkeeper who says he paid workers at the employer's instruction. Shav Yaakov therefore finds the comparison to a doubt arising in one party's domain difficult unless the seller himself was uncertain whether the full hundred kor remained at the moment the agent received it. Shav Yaakov further discusses a related case involving sacks of grain delivered by ship. The buyer's representative accepted the proper number of sacks without weighing them, and a non-Jew later asserted that their total weight was deficient by the equivalent of seventy sacks. The seller stated that he had weighed them properly before handing them to the boatmen. The court ruled for the seller, because the buyer admitted receiving the correct number and had only a doubtful claim about the weight. The seller was required to affirm before beit din that he delivered the proper weight to the boatmen, while the buyer was to bear the reasonable costs of pursuing the boatmen in civil court. The responsum adds a second ground: even if the deficiency arose while the goods were with the carriers, the buyer or his agent was negligent in accepting the sacks without weighing them when scales had been provided. He thereby caused his own loss. Ultimately, because the buyer's claim was doubtful and the seller asserted definite payment through the goods delivered, the seller was technically exempt even from a hesset oath; nevertheless, due to the large amount involved, the court required a solemn affirmation to satisfy the buyer. turei_zahav.en: (Seif 1: whoever's domain the doubt arose in, and so forth.) This wording appears in the Gemara, but the Rif and Rambam disagree with Tosafot and the Rosh regarding its interpretation. The Rif and Rambam explain that it refers literally to the physical domain, meaning the place in which the animal was located, so that the loss falls upon the owner of the donkey if it died in his house. The alternative opinion, that of Tosafot and the Rosh, explains that it does not refer to the physical location but to the legal domain of the owner of the property, namely the owner of the cow, into whose ownership the donkey entered from the moment the donkey's owner drew the cow. One should not ask that, according to this, in the preceding siman, seif 1, where there is doubt as to when the cow gave birth, if the calf is in the possession of the cow's owner, the donkey's owner should have to bring proof, since the doubt arose after he drew the donkey and the cow had already been acquired by the donkey's owner, so the doubt arose in his domain and the burden of proof should rest upon him. Tosafot already addressed this in chapter HaMadir: “One must distinguish between a doubt that arose to one's advantage, as there, and a doubt that arose to one's detriment, as here.” The Sema in seif katan 3 raised this question and strained to find an answer, but these words of Tosafot escaped his notice.

לא נתן לא יתן:
ketzot_hachoshen.en: For the doubt arose in his domain. Suppose goods were stolen or lost after the parties completed their commercial acquisition through the customary handshake, but it is unknown whether the theft occurred before or after the kinyan. It would seem that the purchaser must pay because the party in whose domain the doubt arose bears the burden of proof. Yet perhaps that rule applies only where there is a bodily presumption, as in the cases of a possible tereifah or physical defect. There we say that a body retains its prior status and do not transfer a change from one domain to another. Therefore, if the defect is found in the purchaser's domain, we assume the body changed there unless he proves otherwise. Theft and loss are different. There is indeed a general presumption that property remains where it was, but that is weaker than a bodily presumption. Where the purchaser holds the purchase money, such a weaker presumption should not be enough to extract money from him. There is proof from Rambam in the law of a three party transfer. If Reuven owed Shimon a maneh, Shimon transferred the debt to Levi, and Reuven later proved insolvent, Levi claims that Reuven was already poor and Shimon deceived him, while Shimon says he had been solvent. Rambam places the burden on Shimon to prove solvency. If the general rule were that whoever's domain contained the later discovered uncertainty bears the burden, Levi should have to prove prior poverty. The fact that the loan was documented does not alter the conceptual point, for the bodily presumption rule can compel a purchaser to pay even where money is being extracted. Mordechai concerning a coat that later became cheaper makes the same distinction. He rejects analogy to a slaughtered animal because there the seller is supported by a bodily presumption that the animal was not a tereifah. A market price, however, is naturally subject to change and has no comparable bodily presumption. Even if theft and loss involve some status quo presumption, the bodily presumption is stronger and uniquely capable of supporting extraction. The Tosefta states expressly that if a cow was sold and stolen and each party says it was stolen in the other's domain, they divide; if the thief is later found and the issue is who receives double payment, they divide that too. The Tosefta follows Sumchus, who divides doubtful money. According to the Sages, the one seeking to extract bears the burden, and if the purchaser has not yet paid he need not pay. This proves that the special rule of "the doubt arose in his domain" does not govern ordinary theft or loss.

rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [Rama] That he did not know of the defects. Note: Where one party should have known and the other could not have known, he may not collect without an oath.
